editorialIntro: Most teams don't have an AI problem. They have twelve half-ideas and no way to rank them. The Strategy Sprint replaces that noise with a scored, sequenced plan: where AI earns its keep, in what order, and what to leave alone.

editorialSections.title: Owners and operators who are done guessing

blocks.text: You run a small or mid-size business, a professional practice, or a team inside a larger org. You keep hearing that you should "use AI," you've tried a few things, and none of it has stuck. You don't need another demo. You need someone to look at how you actually operate and tell you the truth about where this technology pays off and where it will waste your money.

items: You have 5–200 people and real workflows worth mapping.
You want a decision, not a science project.
You'd rather spend two weeks getting it right than two quarters drifting.

editorialSections.title: Adoption stalls when nobody has ranked the work

blocks.text: Without a roadmap, AI spending scatters. One person builds a clever prompt, another buys a tool nobody adopts, a third pilot quietly dies. There's no shared view of which processes are high-volume, low-risk, and genuinely improvable — the only combination worth automating first.

The Sprint fixes the sequencing problem. We inventory your workflows, score each candidate on impact, effort, and risk, and hand you an ordered plan. You stop spreading effort thin and start compounding wins in the right order.

editorialSections.title: A structured audit, run with you

blocks.text: Discovery interviews
Two to four working sessions with you and the people who own the workflows, so the plan reflects how the business really runs — not an org chart.
Workflow inventory
A mapped list of repeatable processes across your team, with volume, time cost, and sensitivity noted for each.
Opportunity scoring
Every candidate scored on impact, effort, and risk using a transparent rubric you keep. No black boxes.
Risk and guardrail review
A first pass on where confidentiality, accuracy, or disclosure obligations mean AI needs limits — or shouldn't be used at all.
Tooling recommendation
A grounded view of which tools fit your budget, data posture, and team, with honest trade-offs.
Roadmap readout
A live walkthrough of the sequenced plan so your team leaves aligned, not just emailed a PDF.

editorialSections.title: What you keep at the end

items: A written AI roadmap: prioritized initiatives, sequenced across the next one to three quarters.
The scored opportunity matrix, so you can re-rank as things change.
A tooling shortlist with fit notes and rough cost ranges.
A one-page risk summary flagging where to slow down or bring in a professional.
A recorded readout and your slides, yours to keep and share internally.

blocks.text: You own everything. If you never work with us again, the roadmap still stands on its own. That's the point.

editorialSections.title: Pick the depth that fits

blocks.text: One-week focused audit
A single workflow area or department. Fastest path to a decision when the scope is already narrow.

The default. Full workflow inventory, scoring, risk pass, and readout across the business.

blocks.text: Great fit: a services firm, agency, clinic, or operations team with recurring manual work and a genuine intent to change how it runs. You have a budget owner in the room and can commit a few hours of your team's time over two weeks.

Not the right fit yet: if you already know exactly what to build and just need it built, skip the Sprint and go straight to Workflow Design or Implementation. If you're just curious, the free University will take you a long way first.

editorialIntro: Half of failed AI projects fail at the whiteboard, not in the code. Workflow Design produces the blueprint — every step, prompt, checkpoint, and human review defined — so what gets built is worth building. Your team can run it, or hand it to any developer.

editorialSections.title: Teams with one process worth getting right

blocks.text: You've identified the work you want AI to help with — intake, content, reporting, support triage — and now you need it specified properly before money goes into a build. Maybe you have a developer waiting for a brief. Maybe you want your own team to run it by hand first. Either way, you need the design nailed down.

items: You know the workflow you want to improve.
You want the messy parts — edge cases, review, failure handling — thought through up front.
You'd rather pay for a good blueprint than pay twice for a bad build.

editorialSections.title: "Just automate it" skips the hard 20%

blocks.text: The demo always looks easy. The reality is the exceptions: the client email that doesn't fit the template, the draft that needs a human eye before it goes out, the case where the AI should stop and ask instead of guessing. Skip that thinking and you ship a workflow that works on the happy path and quietly breaks on everything else.

Workflow Design front-loads that thinking. We map the full path, define exactly where AI acts and where a person decides, write the prompts and rules, and specify what happens when things go sideways — so the build inherits a design that already survived contact with reality.

blocks.text: Current-state mapping

Prompt & rule authoring

Review & checkpoint design
Where a person signs off, what they check, and how errors get caught before they reach a client.
Failure & escalation paths
What the workflow does when it's unsure — stop, flag, or route to a human — so it degrades safely.
Build handoff brief
A spec any competent developer (or our Implementation team) can build from without guessing.

editorialSections.title: The gap between "we should" and "it works"

blocks.text: Plenty of teams have a good AI idea and no clean way to ship it. The internal build stalls between other priorities. The freelancer delivers something that works once and nobody can maintain. The tool gets configured badly and quietly produces wrong answers that no one catches.

Implementation closes that gap with a disciplined build: configured to your design, tested against real inputs and edge cases, wrapped in the review checkpoints that keep it safe, and documented so your team can operate and change it. We build it to be handed over — not to keep you dependent.

editorialIntro: Your team is already using AI, whether you've approved it or not. Governance turns that quiet risk into a stated policy: what's allowed, what data can go where, when to disclose, and who reviews what — clear enough to follow and defensible enough to stand behind.

editorialSections.title: Leaders accountable for what the team ships

blocks.text: You're responsible for client confidentiality, quality, or a regulated obligation — and AI now touches work that carries those duties. You want your people to use it, but on rails: no client data pasted into random tools, no AI-generated claims going out unchecked, no disclosure gap you can't explain later.

items: You handle sensitive information — client, patient, financial, or proprietary.
Your team is using AI ahead of any policy, and you know it.
You need something practical people will actually follow, not a binder that gathers dust.

editorialSections.title: "Shadow AI" is the real exposure

blocks.text: Ban it and people use it anyway, out of sight. Ignore it and confidential material ends up in tools that train on it, hallucinated facts reach clients, and no one can say who checked what. The exposure isn't the technology — it's the absence of rules and the absence of a paper trail.

This engagement replaces that vacuum with a clear, usable framework: an acceptable-use policy, concrete data-handling rules, disclosure standards, and a lightweight review process. Adoption becomes deliberate and consistent instead of hidden and risky.

This is practical operational governance, not legal advice. RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney. Where your obligations are legally binding — regulated industries, specific compliance regimes — we'll say so plainly and recommend you run the policy past qualified counsel before you rely on it.
